definition: Decentralized means organized so that control and decision-making are spread among many local points instead of concentrated in one center.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word decentralized. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know decentralized should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The relief effort stayed decentralized on purpose — forty church basements, each dispatching its own trucks, and no headquarters to wait on.

Delegated is weaker than decentralized: delegated tasks are handed down while the center still decides and can take them back, but in a decentralized system the deciding itself lives out at the edges.
Fragmented goes further than decentralized: a decentralized network still coordinates around shared standards, while a fragmented one has splintered — no center, and no common ground either.

Dispersed says only that things are spread out — seeds, crowds, and offices can all be dispersed across a map. Decentralized makes a claim about control: not where the pieces sit, but that the deciding happens at many points instead of one.
Devolved names the handover — power formally passed down from a central government to regional bodies. Decentralized names the resulting shape: however the power got there, no single center holds it.

Decentralized means organized so that control and decision-making are spread among many local points instead of concentrated in one center.
For its first century, the bank ran everything from one marble building: every loan in the region needed a signature from the third floor.
The new charter decentralized it.

Branch managers in two hundred towns now approve loans on their own authority, set their own hours, and answer for their own books; the old headquarters keeps the vault and the archives, but the deciding happens everywhere else.
Decentralized is the exact word for the bank's new shape because the change is about where control lives, not where the buildings are.
The branches always existed; what moved was authority — out of one center and into two hundred local hands.
That undoing of a single center is the de- doing its work: centralize gathered the power in, and decentralize scatters it back out.

Decentralized describes systems, and its claim is always about where decisions are made.

Keep two neighbors straight: a single branch that governs itself is autonomous — decentralized describes the whole arrangement, many self-governing points at once — and a network that has lost its shared standards altogether is not decentralized but fragmented.
Note what the word does not say: a company can scatter offices across five time zones and stay rigidly centralized, so long as every choice still routes through one desk.

When the hurricane took out the county's cell towers, the amateur radio club's old plan finally got its test.
The network they had built was decentralized on principle.
Every operator's garage rig could pass messages to any other; none of them was the hub.
Emergency managers, used to phone systems with a switching center, kept asking which station was 'in charge' so they could route around a failure.
The answer — none of them — turned out to be the point.
Two stations flooded that night, and traffic simply flowed along other paths.
By morning, the club had relayed four hundred messages without a single one passing through any central point.
